name: Peak lapel jacket

lead: A peak lapel jacket has lapel edges that sweep up and outward in a point, instead of the stepped notch of a standard suit. The upward lines are the reason it is chosen for looks: they lead the eye toward the shoulders and give a sharper, more formal outline.

It began as the most formal lapel style, used on double-breasted jackets, tailcoats and many tuxedos, and became fashionable on single-breasted jackets in the late 1920s and 1930s. Menswear writers recommend it for people who want broader-looking shoulders; no formal studies measure that effect.

paras: People pick a peak lapel on a suit jacket, blazer or tuxedo and have it tailored to fit the shoulders, since the cut is demanding to get right. It is worn with a shirt and tie for formal or business occasions or as a statement piece on an otherwise plain outfit.
There is no health risk. Peak lapels read as more formal and bolder, so they can look out of place at casual events, and a poorly cut peak on a single-breasted jacket is regarded as hard to execute.

chain: Lapel edges point upward and outward
Eye follows the line toward the shoulders
Upper body reads broader and sharper
angle.text: The cut is used as an optical device rather than structural change. It pairs with a well-fitted, structured shoulder to emphasise the chest-to-waist taper.

lead: A peak (or peaked) lapel is a jacket lapel whose outer edge points upward toward the shoulder, in contrast to the notched lapel whose edge is cut at an angle to the collar. The upward-pointing line is the main reason it is used in looksmaxxing and style circles: it lengthens the visual line across the chest and shoulders and is said to suggest a broader upper body.[1]

Historically the peak lapel is the most formal lapel. It appears on double-breasted jackets, tailcoats, morning coats and often tuxedos, and the single-breasted peaked jacket was considered very stylish in the late 1920s and 1930s.[1] Wikipedia notes that cutting a good peak on a single-breasted suit is one of tailoring's most challenging tasks.[1]

On bodybuilding forum T Nation, members trading suit advice discuss jacket details such as button count and lapel style; one poster recommending one or two buttons and a notched lapel for general wear shows how these choices are debated as part of dressing the frame.[2]

paras: The notched lapel was the first type of lapel to appear and is the common choice on single-breasted suits and blazers. The peak lapel instead points upward and is the most formal style [1].

Style discussion centres on proportion. Posters and writers favour structured shoulders and lapels that guide the eye outward, and some dress advice on forums favours simple jackets with clean lines for broad-shouldered builds [2]. Claims that a peak lapel specifically widens the shoulders are made by style commentators rather than tested in studies.

timeline.event: The single-breasted peaked jacket becomes highly fashionable [1].
